title: Two norms on C([0,1]): why no constant works
objective: See, curve by curve, why the sup norm and the integral norm are not equivalent on C([0,1]), and which hypothesis of the finite-dimensional theorem fails.

scenes.title: The family
scenes.caption: On [0,1] the functions x to the n are continuous. As n grows they stay near zero except close to x = 1.
scenes.plotDescription: Four increasing curves from (0,0) to (1,1): the line y = x, then x², x⁵ and x²⁰, each lower and flatter on most of the interval before rising steeply near x = 1.

scenes.title: The sup norm sees the peak
scenes.caption: Every curve reaches the value 1 at x = 1, so the sup norm of x to the n is 1 for every n.
scenes.plotDescription: The curves x² and x²⁰, both ending at height 1 when x = 1.

scenes.title: The integral norm sees the area
scenes.caption: The shaded area under x to the 20 is one twenty-first. In general the integral norm is 1 over n plus 1, which tends to 0.
scenes.plotDescription: The curve x²⁰ with the thin region beneath it shaded; the region hugs the right-hand edge and has area 1/21.

scenes.title: No constant can work
scenes.caption: A bound of the sup norm by C times the integral norm would need n + 1 to be at most C for every n. No constant does that.

scenes.title: Which hypothesis fails
scenes.caption: So the two norms are not equivalent on C([0,1]). All norms are equivalent only in finite dimension, and the functions x to the n are linearly independent, so C([0,1]) is infinite-dimensional.
